title: Issues Navigable Waters Protection Rule
description_short: EPA and the Army Corps issued the Navigable Waters Protection Rule, narrowing federal Clean Water Act protections.
description_medium: The Environmental Protection Agency and Army Corps issued the Navigable Waters Protection Rule on April 21, 2020. The rule narrowed which waters fell under federal Clean Water Act protections, changing the reach of federal permitting and pollution controls. Its supporters described it as clarifying jurisdiction; critics warned that fewer waterways would be protected.
description_long: On April 21, 2020, the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers issued the Navigable Waters Protection Rule, narrowing the federal definition of waters covered by the Clean Water Act. That change reduced the waterways subject to federal permitting and pollution controls, shifting more responsibility to state and local governments. The agencies said the rule clarified the statute’s reach; environmental groups warned that streams and wetlands left outside the definition would lose federal safeguards. The dispute mattered because the definition helped determine which projects required federal review and which pollution limits applied. A narrower scope could ease permitting for some landowners and developers while leaving more waterways to state law. The rule became a major point of conflict over federal authority and the balance between development and water protection.

description_short: Judge Arthur Engoron issued a gag order after Trump posted a disparaging comment about the judge’s law clerk.

description_long: On October 3, 2023, Judge Arthur Engoron barred Donald Trump from making public statements about court staff involved in New York’s civil-fraud trial. description_short: Trump repeatedly called press fake news and enemy of the people, escalating attacks on free press and journalism.

description_long: On February 26, 2026, The Guardian reported that the Justice Department had not released three FBI memos documenting four 2019 interviews with a woman who made unsubstantiated allegations that Donald Trump sexually abused her as a minor with Jeffrey Epstein’s assistance. The Guardian said it obtained and reviewed the missing reports, and an administration official confirmed they were authentic. The woman’s claims have not been corroborated; the FBI brought no charges related to them, and some details conflict with what is known about Epstein’s life in the early 1980s. Trump has denied wrongdoing. The department said the documents were duplicative or privileged, while Democrats on the House Oversight Committee demanded an accounting of why they were withheld. title: Trump Claims Absolute Presidential Immunity from Prosecution
description_short: Trump Claims Absolute Presidential Immunity from Prosecution
description_medium: In October 2023, Trump legal team made the unprecedented argument that a former president has absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for any official acts taken while in office. Judge Tanya Chutkan rejected the argument in the DC Jan 6 case, writing that presidents are not kings. Trump appealed to the DC Circuit and ultimately the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case and delayed the trial indefinitely. Legal scholars called the immunity claim the most sweeping assertion of executive power in American history.
description_long: In October 2023, Donald Trump’s lawyers argued that a former president had absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts taken while in office. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan rejected the claim in the federal January 6 case, and the D.C. Circuit affirmed that decision. The Supreme Court agreed to hear Trump’s appeal, delaying the trial while it considered the scope of presidential immunity. In 2024, the Court held that former presidents have absolute immunity for core constitutional powers, presumptive immunity for other official acts, and no immunity for unofficial acts. The ruling returned the case to lower courts to determine which allegations involved official conduct. The dispute raised a major constitutional question: how to protect executive decision-making without placing a former president beyond criminal law. The distinction between official and private actions became central to the prosecution and to future cases involving presidential conduct.

title: Labor Union Decertification Campaign - Anti-Worker 'Right-to-Work' Expansion
description_short: Labor Union Decertification Campaign - Anti-Worker 'Right-to-Work' Expansion
description_medium: Project 2025 proposed changes to labor rules that could make union decertification easier and limit project labor agreements. description_long: Donald Trump implemented Project 2025's systematic campaign to 'weaken unions or make life tougher for them in at least a dozen ways' by facilitating decertification votes anytime union contracts are in force, eliminating project labor agreements, and promoting National Right-to-Work laws that allow non-union workers to benefit from union contracts without paying dues. title: COVID Death Toll Denial - 'It Is What It Is'
description_short: COVID Death Toll Denial - 'It Is What It Is'
description_medium: During an August 2020 Axios interview about the rising U.S. COVID-19 death toll, Donald Trump responded, “It is what it is.” The exchange became a flashpoint in debate over his public response to the pandemic, as deaths continued to rise and families mourned losses across the country. The remark drew criticism for its blunt response to the growing toll.
description_long: When confronted with America's rising COVID-19 death toll during an August 2020 Axios interview, Donald Trump callously dismissed the tragedy by saying 'It is what it is,' encapsulating his administration's indifference to the hundreds of thousands of Americans dying from the pandemic. As the U.S. death toll approached and then exceeded 400,000 by the end of his presidency, Trump consistently downplayed the severity, refused to take responsibility, and spread misinformation that contributed to preventable deaths. Trump repeatedly compared COVID deaths to car accidents, heart disease, and other causes of death to minimize the pandemic's impact, arguing that the media was unfairly focusing on COVID fatalities. He claimed the U.S. had 'one of the lowest death rates in the world' when it actually had one of the highest death rates among developed nations. Trump's 'it is what it is' comment became emblematic of his callous indifference to American suffering and his inability to provide compassionate leadership during a national crisis. The phrase was widely seen as disqualifying for a president, demonstrating his complete lack of empathy for grieving families and his treatment of mass death as a political inconvenience rather than a human tragedy. Trump's COVID death toll denial extended to pressuring officials to change death certificates, claiming hospitals were inflating COVID deaths for profit, and suggesting that deaths 'with COVID' shouldn't count as deaths 'from COVID.' His administration's failure to implement a coordinated national response, combined with his public undermining of health experts and safety measures, contributed to America having one of the world's worst pandemic outcomes despite having advanced medical capabilities.

title: Content Moderation Elimination - Social Media Disinformation Protection System
description_short: Content Moderation Elimination - Social Media Disinformation Protection System
description_medium: Project 2025 proposals affecting Section 230 and Meta’s 2025 moderation changes fueled concerns about election misinformation and online fact-checking. Project 2025's content regulation approach established government control over online speech by eliminating private companies' editorial discretion while protecting disinformation that benefited Trump's political agenda, effectively creating state-sponsored information warfare that privileged false political claims over factual accuracy. The social media transformation represented what democracy advocates called 'aims to derail efforts to stop election disinformation' by eliminating independent fact-checking while using federal law enforcement to persecute organizations that provided accurate information about elections and democratic processes, completing transformation of information ecosystem into propaganda distribution system.
